feedback: If the shape has the wrong number of sides, recount together, marking each side exactly once from a clear start point; dotted paper or pegs keep sides straight.
If only a regular/symmetrical version is produced, prompt: 'Make one that is squished, tilted, or spiky but still has five straight sides' and affirm that it counts just as much.
If the figure has a gap or a curved/bulging edge, check it against the attributes aloud: is it closed? is every side straight?
Celebrate an irregular valid solution explicitly so the learner sees it is as correct as the neat one.
activities.intendedInsight: A polygon class is defined by its attribute (number of straight sides meeting at vertices, closed figure with sides that do not cross), invariant to size, orientation and regularity — not by matching a single remembered prototype.
learnerActions: Given an instruction such as 'build a shape with exactly five straight sides', construct the figure on dotted paper, a geoboard, or a peg/rubber-band grid.
Count and mark each side (and vertex) once as it is drawn, so the total is checked rather than guessed.
Ensure the figure CLOSES and that every side is straight before declaring it finished.
When one valid shape is made, draw 'a different pentagon that does NOT look like the first one' — a long, spiky, or irregular one.
Compare a regular and an irregular example of the same class side by side and state why both satisfy the attribute.
activities.title: Build a polygon to a target side-count

feedback: If an irregular or tilted member is skipped, draw attention to it and recount its sides together; attending to the awkward four-sided shape is intended to loosen the prototype grip as the learner sees the squished one also counts.
If a shape is included or excluded by its name/look alone (e.g. 'that's a diamond, not a quadrilateral'), redirect to counting the four straight sides.
If counting on an irregular shape loses track, model starting at one vertex and marking each side once around the figure.
activities.intendedInsight: Identifying a class means applying its attribute to every candidate, including irregular and rotated ones, rather than recognising a familiar picture.
learnerActions: From a mixed set that includes regular, irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples, mark EVERY member of a named class (e.g. 'circle all the quadrilaterals').
For each shape marked or skipped, justify by counting sides/vertices and checking closed + straight-sided, not by its name or look.
Deliberately inspect the awkward shapes — a long thin tilted four-sided shape, a dented pentagon — and decide membership by the attribute.
Explain why a square is a quadrilateral, and why a 'diamond' is also a quadrilateral regardless of its orientation.
activities.title: Find them all in a mixed set

feedback: If the count is wrong, recount marking each side/vertex once; dotted paper keeps the sides straight.
If both drawings look the same, ask for a genuinely different-looking version with the same number of sides.
Accept and praise any closed, straight-sided figure with the correct count regardless of regularity.
activities.intendedInsight: Justifying class membership by the attribute count — and producing a non-prototypical second example — demonstrates the definition is understood, not just a remembered shape.
learnerActions: Draw a named polygon (e.g. a hexagon) and explain how you know it is one by counting its six straight sides and six vertices/angles.
Produce a second example of the same name that looks clearly different from the first.
State the defining attributes in your own words ('a hexagon is any closed shape with six straight sides that do not cross each other').
activities.title: Name, draw and justify by attribute
